title: The boy at the door
hook: Parvati shapes a son from earth and breathes life into him; why families welcome Ganesha into clay
carry: the holy can live in clay
tomorrow: the boy says no to the next one at the door. who is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the first camp on a battlefield, with Krishna's line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Now the stories start, and the first one starts at a closed door.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Parvati lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and every guard at the door is one of his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants in, they step aside. Nobody in that house is simply hers. So before her bath she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin, the earth of her own body, and shapes a boy. Then she breathes life into him. The first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff and gives him one job: guard this door. No one comes in.
screen: `NOBODY IN THE HOUSE IS HERS.` → `A BOY SHAPED FROM EARTH.` → `SHE BREATHES LIFE INTO HIM.` → `NO ONE COMES IN.`

segments.voice: That boy grows up to be Ganesha, the god you met on day one. This telling is the Shiva Purana's, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version. Notice what he's made of. Not thunder, not light. Earth, shaped by the Goddess's hands, with her breath in it. Hindu homes still act this story out. Every year at Ganesh Chaturthi, many families bring home a Ganesha shaped from clay. With prayers they invite him to live in it, a rite called prana pratishtha: setting the breath in. For a few days he's the guest of honor, fed, sung to, visited by the whole street. Then they carry him to a river or the sea, and give the clay back to the water. The teaching under it: God can be welcomed into something as ordinary as earth, and loved there, without being trapped there. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: God isn't only far off in the sky. God can be found in what's right in front of you, even a handful of earth. And somewhere down the mountain, someone very large is walking home.
screen: `EARTH, SHAPED BY THE GODDESS.` · `GANESH CHATURTHI: A GOD OF CLAY.` · `PRANA PRATISHTHA: SETTING THE BREATH IN.` · `BACK TO THE WATER.` · then, large: `THE HOLY CAN LIVE IN CLAY.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, pick up something ordinary near you that matters to you: a ring, a mug, a photo. Hold it. Notice that it's just stuff, and also not. Something you love has been breathed into it. Then set it down gently. It's still yours.
Ganas: Shiva's attendants, the guards of his house. Keep an eye on them. The boy made of earth is going to end up leading them.
Your line: the holy can live in clay. Parvati shaped hers from earth. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO WALKS UP TO THAT DOOR?`

howItsDone: At Ganesh Chaturthi many families bring home a clay Ganesha, invite him in with prana pratishtha, and after a day and a half to ten days immerse the image in water (visarjan). His birth story is often retold then.

fork.setup: a friend asks: if you put the clay Ganesha in the ocean, was he ever really god? what fits today's teaching?
options: for many Hindus, the clay was his home for a while. he isn't lost when it goes back to the water.
no, it was only ever decoration.
yes, so the clay should never be put in the water.
fork.reveal: families invite Ganesha in with prayer and later bid him farewell. the image is holy for a time; letting it go doesn't let God go.

original.note: Sanskrit: lord (isha) of the ganas, the attendants. The boy at the door grows into their leader.

ganas.meaning: Shiva's attendants, who guard his house

Parvati.meaning: the goddess who lives with Shiva; Ganesha's mother

Kailash.meaning: the mountain where Shiva and Parvati live

Ganesha.meaning: the god of beginnings, honored as keeper of thresholds

Shiva Purana.meaning: a collection of stories about Shiva

Ganesh Chaturthi.meaning: the yearly festival of Ganesha's birth

prana pratishtha.meaning: the rite of inviting the god's life into an image

visarjan.meaning: giving the image back to the water at the festival's end

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda (the birth of Ganesha)
Ganesh Chaturthi household practice: prana pratishtha and visarjan
